claims.text: Post-sintering annealing will promote short-range ordering at W–Cu interfaces.
Interfacial short-range ordering will increase the overall thermal conductivity of a W–Cu composite.
The proposed annealing and interfacial ordering will preserve the mechanical durability of the W–Cu composite.
The proposed annealing and interfacial ordering will preserve the irradiation resistance of the W–Cu composite.
A conventionally sintered W–Cu composite has disordered interfaces.
An annealing temperature can be chosen that enables sufficient interfacial atomic diffusion without significant grain growth or deleterious phase transformations in W–Cu.
The annealing treatment will form ordered clusters or SRO zones at the interfaces between tungsten and copper phases.
Short-range ordering reduces atomic displacements and lattice distortion.
Reduced interfacial disorder decreases phonon scattering at W–Cu boundaries.
Reduced interfacial disorder decreases electron scattering at W–Cu boundaries.
Interfacial SRO improves bonding between the tungsten and copper phases.
The annealing treatment leaves the mechanically durable and irradiation-resistant phases intact.
The annealed W–Cu composite will have approximately 10–15% higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable unannealed composite.
The annealed composite will show minimal degradation in mechanical strength.
The annealed composite will show minimal degradation in irradiation resistance.
In equiatomic bcc HfNbTaTiZr, maximum SRO increased lattice thermal conductivity by about 12% relative to the random alloy.
The induced interfacial order will remain stable under moderate operating temperatures and irradiation doses typical of heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joints.
Extreme thermal or irradiation conditions could alter the microstructure and negate the conductivity benefit.
